title: Origins of Sociology
description: Comte, Saint-Simon, Spencer, and the 19th-century context that birthed the discipline

concepts.title: The 19th-Century Context
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociology was forged in the upheavals of the 19th century. Two great revolutions reshaped Europe: the French Revolution (1789) shattered the ancien régime and raised urgent questions about social order, legitimacy, and equality, while the Industrial Revolution uprooted peasants into crowded factory cities, producing new classes, new miseries, and new forms of solidarity.

Traditional explanations — theology, divine right, natural law — could no longer account for societies in such rapid flux. Thinkers asked: what holds modern society together? What replaces the church, the guild, the village? Could a science of society be built on the model of physics or biology?

The answer was sociology: a self-consciously scientific study of social life, born from the need to understand modernity itself. Its founders saw themselves diagnosing a civilization in crisis — not as detached observers but as physicians of the social body.

concepts.title: Comte and Positivism
concepts.contentHtml:
Auguste Comte (1798–1857) coined the term sociologie in 1838 and proposed it as the queen of sciences — the most complex, sitting atop a hierarchy that began with mathematics and rose through physics, chemistry, and biology.

Comte's law of three stages claimed that human thought passes from the theological (events explained by gods), through the metaphysical (abstract forces), to the positive stage — in which knowledge is grounded in observation and the discovery of empirical laws. Sociology was to apply positive method to society itself.

His former mentor Henri de Saint-Simon (1760–1825) had already argued that industrial society needed a new moral and scientific elite to replace priests and nobles. Comte systematised this vision into a programme: knowledge for prediction, prediction for control, control for reform. He even tried, late in life, to found a 'religion of humanity' as a positivist substitute for Christianity.

concepts.title: Spencer and Social Evolutionism
concepts.contentHtml:
Herbert Spencer (1820–1903) was the leading English social theorist of his generation and arguably more influential than Comte in his lifetime. Inspired partly by pre-Darwinian biology, he treated society as an organism that evolved from simple, homogeneous forms toward complex, differentiated ones.

It was Spencer, not Darwin, who coined the phrase 'survival of the fittest' (1864). He extended evolutionary thinking into ethics and politics, arguing for laissez-faire: state interference in welfare or markets distorted natural selection within society.

This social Darwinism — though the label is a later one — had enormous reach in late-Victorian Britain and Gilded Age America, lending pseudo-scientific authority to inequality. Later sociologists (Durkheim, Weber) defined themselves partly against Spencer's individualist organicism, but the question he raised — how does society differentiate? — remained central to Durkheim's Division of Labor and beyond.

title: Karl Marx
description: Historical materialism, alienation, class struggle, and the critique of capital

concepts.title: Historical Materialism
concepts.contentHtml:
Karl Marx (1818–1883), with Friedrich Engels, developed historical materialism: the claim that the economic organisation of production — the mode of production — is the foundation on which legal, political, and ideological life rests.

The famous metaphor from the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy distinguishes the base (forces and relations of production) from the superstructure (law, politics, religion, philosophy). 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but, on the contrary, their social being that determines their consciousness.'

History is the succession of modes of production — ancient slave society, feudalism, capitalism — each containing internal contradictions that drive its transformation. The motor of this transformation is class struggle: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (Communist Manifesto, 1848).

concepts.title: Alienation
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 — unpublished in Marx's lifetime, recovered in 1932 — the young Marx develops his theory of alienation (Entfremdung) under capitalism.

The wage labourer is alienated in four ways: from the product of labour (which belongs to the capitalist); from the act of labour (which is forced, monotonous, externally controlled); from species-being (the distinctively human capacity for free, creative, self-directed activity); and from other workers (turned into competitors in the labour market).

Labour, which should be the realisation of human nature, becomes its negation. Work is not a sphere of self-expression but a means to the wage that lets one survive outside work. The 1844 Manuscripts gave 20th-century Marxism a humanist register that reinvigorated the tradition during the Cold War — especially in the work of the Frankfurt School and the early Erich Fromm.

concepts.title: Capital, Commodity Fetishism, and Ideology
concepts.contentHtml:
In Capital, Volume 1 (1867), Marx analyses the capitalist mode of production through the labour theory of value. Workers produce more value than they receive in wages; the difference is surplus value, the source of profit. Exploitation is structural, not personal — it operates even where individual capitalists are kind.

Commodity fetishism describes how, under capitalism, social relations between people appear as objective relations between things. The price of a coat seems to inhere in the coat itself, hiding the labour and class relations that produced it. Markets present themselves as natural facts.

Ideology, in The German Ideology (1846), names the systematic distortions through which the ruling class presents its particular interests as the universal interest. Religion, classical political economy, even much philosophy function ideologically — not by lying outright, but by naturalising what is historical and contingent.

title: Émile Durkheim
description: Social facts, solidarity, anomie, and the sociology of religion

concepts.title: Social Facts and Solidarity
concepts.contentHtml:
Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) wanted to establish sociology as a rigorous, autonomous science. In The Rules of Sociological Method (1895) he defined its object: the social fact — a way of acting, thinking, or feeling that is external to individuals and exerts coercive power over them. Language, law, currency, and morality are social facts: they exist before any individual and constrain behaviour.

His doctoral thesis The Division of Labor in Society (1893) traced the historical shift from mechanical solidarity — the cohesion of small, undifferentiated societies bound by shared beliefs and a strong collective conscience — to organic solidarity, the cohesion of complex modern societies bound together by interdependence among specialised roles.

Modern society is not held together by sameness but by mutual need: the doctor, the baker, and the engineer require each other. Punishment changes accordingly — from repressive (vengeful, expressing collective outrage) to restitutive (restoring the disturbed relation between specialists).

concepts.title: Anomie and Suicide
concepts.contentHtml:
When the moral regulation that fits a society's structure breaks down, Durkheim called the result anomie — literally 'without norms'. Rapid economic change, sudden affluence, or sudden ruin can leave individuals without clear standards for what to want or how to live, and human desire, lacking limits, becomes a source of suffering.

In Suicide (1897) Durkheim used statistical method to defend a startling thesis: even an act seemingly as private as suicide is shaped by social facts. He distinguished four types: egoistic (insufficient integration into a group; hence higher rates among Protestants than Catholics), altruistic (excessive integration, e.g. soldiers), anomic (deregulation, e.g. economic crisis), and fatalistic (overregulation, e.g. slaves — mentioned only briefly).

The book is a tour de force of sociological method: a phenomenon at the limit of psychology turns out to vary systematically with the structure of social bonds.

concepts.title: The Elementary Forms of Religious Life
concepts.contentHtml:
In his last major work, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), Durkheim studied Aboriginal Australian totemism as the simplest form of religion in order to uncover the function of religion in general.

His thesis: religion is society worshipping itself. The sacred is not a delusion but a real force — the power of the collectivity over the individual, made visible through symbols, rituals, and the totem. The collective effervescence of ritual gatherings generates and renews the moral bonds of the group; we feel in such moments that we are in the presence of something greater than ourselves, and we are — we are in the presence of society.

The distinction between sacred and profane — not gods, not the supernatural — is the universal core of religion. This functionalist account inaugurated the sociology of religion and influenced anthropologists from Mauss to Lévi-Strauss to Mary Douglas. Durkheim's broader legacy is the insistence that society is a reality sui generis, irreducible to individual psychology.

title: Max Weber
description: Verstehen, the Protestant Ethic, authority, and the iron cage of bureaucracy

concepts.title: Verstehen and Ideal Types
concepts.contentHtml:
Max Weber (1864–1920) defined sociology as the science that seeks interpretive understanding — Verstehen — of social action in order to causally explain its course and effects. Where Durkheim treated social facts as things to be observed externally, Weber insisted that sociology must grasp the subjective meanings agents attach to their conduct.

To handle the complexity of meaningful action, Weber developed the ideal type: a deliberately one-sided conceptual construction that accentuates certain features of reality to make them intelligible. 'The bureaucratic official', 'the Protestant entrepreneur', 'charismatic authority' are not descriptions of any actual case but yardsticks against which actual cases can be measured.

This methodology made Weberian sociology distinctive: causal but humanistic, comparative but attentive to particulars, rigorous but acknowledging that the social scientist always selects what to study from infinite reality through value-relevance — while striving in the analysis itself for value-freedom.

concepts.title: The Protestant Ethic
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), Weber asked why modern industrial capitalism arose in Western Europe rather than in China or India, which had cities, markets, and money long before. His controversial answer pointed to an elective affinity between ascetic Protestantism — especially Calvinism — and the disciplined, methodical, profit-reinvesting ethos that capitalism requires.

Calvinist predestination made salvation uncertain. Worldly success in a calling came to be read as a possible sign of being among the elect. Combined with the doctrine that consumption beyond modest needs was sinful, this produced the unique combination of relentless work, frugality, and accumulation that we recognise as the spirit of capitalism.

Once capitalism was established, it no longer needed religious motivation; the cage of routine took over. The argument is famously not a refutation of Marx but a deliberate counterweight: ideas, not only material conditions, can shape historical outcomes.

concepts.title: Authority, Bureaucracy, and the Iron Cage
concepts.contentHtml:
Weber distinguished three pure types of legitimate authority: traditional (legitimacy through 'the sanctity of immemorial traditions' — chiefs, monarchs); charismatic (devotion to an extraordinary individual — prophets, revolutionary leaders); and legal-rational (obedience to impersonal rules and the offices that administer them).

Modern states and corporations rest on legal-rational authority, embodied in the bureaucracy: hierarchy, written rules, specialised offices, salaried officials, technical qualification. Bureaucracy is technically the most efficient form of organisation yet devised, but Weber feared its consequences: the relentless rationalisation of life threatens to imprison humanity in an iron cage (stahlhartes Gehäuse) of disenchanted, calculative existence.

Weber also rejected Marx's reduction of stratification to class alone. He distinguished class (economic position in markets), status (social honour and lifestyle), and party (political power) as three independent dimensions of inequality, each capable of moving without the others.

title: Other Classics
description: Simmel, Du Bois, Martineau, Tocqueville — the wider founding canon

concepts.title: Georg Simmel: Form, the Stranger, and the Metropolis
concepts.contentHtml:
Georg Simmel (1858–1918) practised what he called formal sociology: the study of recurring forms of social interaction — conflict, exchange, subordination, sociability — abstracted from their particular contents. Different topics share the same form; the same group can host many forms.

Simmel's analysis of the dyad and triad showed how adding a third party fundamentally changes social dynamics: the third can mediate, divide and rule, or unite the other two against itself. Group size is itself a structural variable. His essay 'The Stranger' (1908) examined the figure who is near and far at once — the trader who arrives and stays, neither fully inside nor outside the group.

In 'The Metropolis and Mental Life' (1903), Simmel argued that urban life produces a blasé attitude as a defence against constant stimulation, while the money economy reduces qualitative differences to quantitative ones, freeing individuals from particular ties but leaving them isolated in a world of indifferent calculation.

concepts.title: W.E.B. Du Bois: Double Consciousness and the Color Line
concepts.contentHtml:
W.E.B. Du Bois (1868–1963) was the first African American to earn a Harvard PhD and produced some of the earliest empirical urban sociology in The Philadelphia Negro (1899). For most of the 20th century white sociology marginalised him; he is now widely recognised as a founding classic.

In The Souls of Black Folk (1903) Du Bois introduced double consciousness: the experience of African Americans of 'always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity.' One feels two-ness — American and Negro — in a single body.

His prediction that 'the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line' framed race as a global structural relation, not a local prejudice. Du Bois extended classical sociology by showing that any account of modernity that ignored slavery, colonialism, and race was radically incomplete — an insight whose force the discipline only fully absorbed decades later.

concepts.title: Martineau and Tocqueville
concepts.contentHtml:
Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) is increasingly recognised as a proto-sociologist. She produced the first English translation of Comte's Positive Philosophy (1853) — condensing him better than the original — and in How to Observe Morals and Manners (1838) wrote what may be the first methodological treatise in sociology, anticipating themes from feminist and qualitative research. Her Society in America (1837) systematically compared American ideals with American practice, including slavery and the position of women.

Alexis de Tocqueville (1805–1859), in Democracy in America (1835/1840), examined the United States as a laboratory of democratic equality. He admired the vitality of American civil associations — voluntary groups he saw as schools of self-government — while warning of a 'tyranny of the majority' and a soft despotism in which equal but isolated citizens trade liberty for comfort.

Tocqueville's questions about democracy, individualism, and association still anchor political sociology today, and Martineau's recovery has reshaped accounts of who counts as a founder of the discipline.
